5.1.1. What is experimental design?




       5. Process Improvement
       5.1. Introduction


       5.1.1. What is experimental design?

       Experimental         In an experiment, we deliberately change one or more process
       Design (or           variables (or factors) in order to observe the effect the changes have
       DOE)                 on one or more response variables. The (statistical) design of
       economically         experiments (DOE) is an efficient procedure for planning experiments
       maximizes            so that the data obtained can be analyzed to yield valid and objective
       information          conclusions.

                            DOE begins with determining the objectives of an experiment and
                            selecting the process factors for the study. An Experimental Design is
                            the laying out of a detailed experimental plan in advance of doing the
                            experiment. Well chosen experimental designs maximize the amount
                            of "information" that can be obtained for a given amount of
                            experimental effort.

                            The statistical theory underlying DOE generally begins with the
                            concept of process models.

                            Process Models for DOE

       Black box            It is common to begin with a process model of the `black box' type,
       process              with several discrete or continuous input factors that can be
       model                controlled--that is, varied at will by the experimenter--and one or
                            more measured output responses. The output responses are assumed
                            continuous. Experimental data are used to derive an empirical
                            (approximation) model linking the outputs and inputs. These
                            empirical models generally contain first and second-order terms.

                            Often the experiment has to account for a number of uncontrolled
                            factors that may be discrete, such as different machines or operators,
                            and/or continuous such as ambient temperature or humidity. Figure
                            1.1 illustrates this situation.

       controlled

       Models for           The most common empirical models fit to the experimental data take

       Linear model         A linear model with two factors, X1 and X2 , can be written as



                            Here, Y is the response for given levels of the main effects X1 and X2
                            and the X1 X2 term is included to account for a possible interaction
                            effect between X1 and X2 . The constant 0 is the response of Y when
                            both main effects are 0.

                            For a more complicated example, a linear model with three factors
                            X1 , X2 , X3 and one response, Y, would look like (if all possible terms
                            were included in the model)




                            The three terms with single "X's" are the main effects terms. There are
                            k(k-1)/2 = 3*2/2 = 3 two-way interaction terms and 1 three-way
                            interaction term (which is often omitted, for simplicity). When the
                            experimental data are analyzed, all the unknown " " parameters are
                            estimated and the coefficients of the "X" terms are tested to see which

                            out of the model.

       5.1.2. What are the uses of DOE?

      DOE is a             Below are seven examples illustrating situations in which experimental design can
      multipurpose         be used effectively:
      tool that can
      help in many                 Choosing Between Alternatives
      situations                   Selecting the Key Factors Affecting a Response
                                   Response Surface Modeling to:
                                         Hit a Target

                           Choosing Between Alternatives (Comparative Experiment)

      A common             Supplier A vs. supplier B? Which new additive is the most effective? Is catalyst `x'
      use is               an improvement over the existing catalyst? These and countless other choices
      planning an          between alternatives can be presented to us in a never-ending parade. Often we have
      experiment           the choice made for us by outside factors over which we have no control. But in
      to gather            many cases we are also asked to make the choice. It helps if one has valid data to
      data to make         back up one's decision.
      a decision
      between two          The preferred solution is to agree on a measurement by which competing choices
      or more              can be compared, generate a sample of data from each alternative, and compare
      alternatives         average results. The 'best' average outcome will be our preference. We have
                           performed a comparative experiment!

      Types of             Sometimes this comparison is performed under one common set of conditions. This
      comparitive          is a comparative study with a narrow scope - which is suitable for some initial
      studies              comparisons of possible alternatives. Other comparison studies, intended to validate
                           that one alternative is perferred over a wide range of conditions, will purposely and
                           systematically vary the background conditions under which the primary comparison
                           is made in order to reach a conclusion that will be proven valid over a broad scope.
                           We discuss experimental designs for each of these types of comparisons in Sections
                           5.3.3.1 and 5.3.3.2.

                           Selecting the Key Factors Affecting a Response (Screening Experiments)

      Selecting the        Often there are many possible factors, some of which may be critical and others
      few that             which may have little or no effect on a response. It may be desirable, as a goal by


http://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/pri/section1/pri12.htm[6/27/2012 2:23:30 PM]
5.1.2. What are the uses of DOE?

      matter from          itself, to reduce the number of factors to a relatively small set (2-5) so that attention
      the many             can be focussed on controlling those factors with appropriate specifications, control
      possible             charts, etc.
      factors
                           Screening experiments are an efficient way, with a minimal number of runs, of
                           determining the important factors. They may also be used as a first step when the
                           ultimate goal is to model a response with a response surface. We will discuss
                           experimental designs for screening a large number of factors in Sections 5.3.3.3,
                           5.3.3.4 and 5.3.3.5.

                           Response Surface Modeling a Process

      Some                 Once one knows the primary variables (factors) that affect the responses of interest,
      reasons to           a number of additional objectives may be pursued. These include:
      model a
      process                      Hitting a Target
                                   Maximizing or Minimizing a Response
                                   Reducing Variation
                                   Making a Process Robust
                                   Seeking Multiple Goals

                           What each of these purposes have in common is that experimentation is used to fit a
                           model that may permit a rough, local approximation to the actual surface. Given that
                           the particular objective can be met with such an approximate model, the
                           experimental effort is kept to a minimum while still achieving the immediate goal.

                           These response surface modeling objectives will now be briefly expanded upon.

                           Hitting a Target

      Often we             This is a frequently encountered goal for an experiment.
      want to "fine
      tune" a              One might try out different settings until the desired target is `hit' consistently. For
      process to           example, a machine tool that has been recently overhauled may require some setup
      consistently         `tweaking' before it runs on target. Such action is a small and common form of
      hit a target         experimentation. However, rather than experimenting in an ad hoc manner until we
                           happen to find a setup that hits the target, one can fit a model estimated from a
                           small experiment and use this model to determine the necessary adjustments to hit
                           the target.

                           More complex forms of experimentation, such as the determination of the correct
                           chemical mix of a coating that will yield a desired refractive index for the dried coat
                           (and simultaneously achieve specifications for other attributes), may involve many
                           ingredients and be very sensitive to small changes in the percentages in the mix.
                           Fitting suitable models, based on sequentially planned experiments, may be the only
                           way to efficiently achieve this goal of hitting targets for multiple responses
                           simultaneously.

                           Maximizing or Minimizing a Response

      Optimizing a         Many processes are being run at sub-optimal settings, some of them for years, even
      process              though each factor has been optimized individually over time. Finding settings that
      output is a          increase yield or decrease the amount of scrap and rework represent opportunities
      common               for substantial financial gain. Often, however, one must experiment with multiple

5.1.2. What are the uses of DOE?

      goal                 inputs to achieve a better output. Section 5.3.3.6 on second-order designs plus
                           material in Section 5.5.3 will be useful for these applications.

      Processes            A process may be performing with unacceptable consistency, meaning its internal

      target, on
      the average,         Excessive variation can result from many causes. Sometimes it is due to the lack of
      may still            having or following standard operating procedures. At other times, excessive
      have too             variation is due to certain hard-to-control inputs that affect the critical output
      much                 characteristics of the process. When this latter situation is the case, one may
      variability          experiment with these hard-to-control factors, looking for a region where the surface
                           is flatter and the process is easier to manage. To take advantage of such flatness in
                           the surface, one must use designs - such as the second-order designs of Section
                           5.3.3.6 - that permit identification of these features. Contour or surface plots are
                           useful for elucidating the key features of these fitted models. See also 5.5.3.1.4.

                           Making a Process Robust

      The less a           An item designed and made under controlled conditions will be later `field tested' in
      process or           the hands of the customer and may prove susceptible to failure modes not seen in
      product is           the lab or thought of by design. An example would be the starter motor of an
      affected by          automobile that is required to operate under extremes of external temperature. A
      external             starter that performs under such a wide range is termed `robust' to temperature.
      conditions,
      the better it        Designing an item so that it is robust calls for a special experimental effort. It is
      is - this is         possible to stress the item in the design lab and so determine the critical components
      called               affecting its performance. A different gauge of armature wire might be a solution to
      "Robustness"         the starter motor, but so might be many other alternatives. The correct combination
                           of factors can be found only by experimentation.

      Sometimes            A product or process seldom has just one desirable output characteristic. There are
      we have              usually several, and they are often interrelated so that improving one will cause a

      we have to           Any product is a trade-off between these various desirable final characteristics.

      Regression           Sometimes we require more than a rough approximating model over a local region.

5.1.3. What are the steps of DOE?




      5. Process Improvement
      5.1. Introduction


       5.1.3. What are the steps of DOE?

      Key steps for           Obtaining good results from a DOE involves these seven
      DOE                     steps:

                                    1. Set objectives
                                    2. Select process variables
                                    3. Select an experimental design
                                    4. Execute the design
                                    5. Check that the data are consistent with the
                                       experimental assumptions
                                    6. Analyze and interpret the results
                                    7. Use/present the results (may lead to further runs or
                                       DOE's).


      A checklist of          Important practical considerations in planning and running
      practical               experiments are
      considerations
                                       Check performance of gauges/measurement devices
                                       first.
                                       Keep the experiment as simple as possible.
                                       Check that all planned runs are feasible.
                                       Watch out for process drifts and shifts during the
                                       run.
                                       Avoid unplanned changes (e.g., swap operators at
                                       halfway point).
                                       Allow some time (and back-up material) for
                                       unexpected events.
                                       Obtain buy-in from all parties involved.
                                       Maintain effective ownership of each step in the
                                       experimental plan.
                                       Preserve all the raw data--do not keep only summary
                                       averages!
                                       Record everything that happens.
                                       Reset equipment to its original state after the
                                       experiment.

       5. Process Improvement
       5.2. Assumptions


        5.2.2. Is the process stable?

       Plan to             Experimental runs should have control runs that are made at
       examine             the `standard' process setpoints, or at least at some standard
       process             operating recipe. The experiment should start and end with
       stability as        such runs. A plot of the outcomes of these control runs will
       part of             indicate if the underlying process itself has drifted or shifted
       your                during the experiment.
       experiment
                           It is desirable to experiment on a stable process. However, if
                           this cannot be achieved, then the process instability must be
                           accounted for in the analysis of the experiment. For example,
                           if the mean is shifting with time (or experimental trial run),
                           then it will be necessary to include a trend term in the
                           experimental model (i.e., include a time variable or a run
                           number variable).

       Polynomial                 In this chapter we restrict ourselves to the case for which the
       approximation              response variable(s) are continuous outputs denoted as Y.
       models only                Over the experimental range, the outputs must not only be
       work for                   continuous, but also reasonably smooth. A sharp falloff in Y
       smoothly                   values is likely to be missed by the approximating
       varying                    polynomials that we use because these polynomials assume a
       outputs                    smoothly curving underlying response surface.

       smoothness                 piecewise smooth, then the experiments will have to be
       requires                   broken up into separate experiments, each investigating the
       separate                   shape of the separate sections. A surface that is known to be
       experiments                very jagged (i.e., non-smooth) will not be successfully
                                  approximated by a smooth polynomial.

5.2.4. Are the model residuals well-behaved?




       5. Process Improvement
       5.2. Assumptions


       5.2.4. Are the model residuals well-behaved?

       Residuals are         Residuals are estimates of experimental error obtained by subtracting the observed
       the                   responses from the predicted responses.
       differences
       between the           The predicted response is calculated from the chosen model, after all the unknown
       observed and          model parameters have been estimated from the experimental data.
       predicted
       responses             Examining residuals is a key part of all statistical modeling, including DOE's.
                             Carefully looking at residuals can tell us whether our assumptions are reasonable
                             and our choice of model is appropriate.

       Residuals are         Residuals can be thought of as elements of variation unexplained by the fitted
       elements of           model. Since this is a form of error, the same general assumptions apply to the
       variation             group of residuals that we typically use for errors in general: one expects them to be
       unexplained           (roughly) normal and (approximately) independently distributed with a mean of 0
       by fitted             and some constant variance.
       model

       Assumptions           These are the assumptions behind ANOVA and classical regression analysis. This
       for residuals         means that an analyst should expect a regression model to err in predicting a
                             response in a random fashion; the model should predict values higher than actual
                             and lower than actual with equal probability. In addition, the level of the error
                             should be independent of when the observation occurred in the study, or the size of
                             the observation being predicted, or even the factor settings involved in making the
                             prediction. The overall pattern of the residuals should be similar to the bell-shaped
                             pattern observed when plotting a histogram of normally distributed data.

                             We emphasize the use of graphical methods to examine residuals.

       Departures            Departures from these assumptions usually mean that the residuals contain structure
       indicate              that is not accounted for in the model. Identifying that structure and adding term(s)
       inadequate            representing it to the original model leads to a better model.
       model

                             Tests for Residual Normality

       Plots for             Any graph suitable for displaying the distribution of a set of data is suitable for
       examining             judging the normality of the distribution of a group of residuals. The three most
       residuals             common types are:

                                 1. histograms,
                                 2. normal probability plots, and
                                 3. dot plots.


http://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/pri/section2/pri24.htm[6/27/2012 2:23:35 PM]
5.2.4. Are the model residuals well-behaved?



       Histogram




                             The histogram is a frequency plot obtained by placing the data in regularly spaced
                             cells and plotting each cell frequency versus the center of the cell. Figure 2.2
                             illustrates an approximately normal distribution of residuals produced by a model for
                             a calibration process. We have superimposed a normal density function on the
                             histogram.

       Small sample          Sample sizes of residuals are generally small (<50) because experiments have
       sizes                 limited treatment combinations, so a histogram is not be the best choice for judging
                             the distribution of residuals. A more sensitive graph is the normal probability plot.

       Normal                The steps in forming a normal probability plot are:
       probability
       plot                          Sort the residuals into ascending order.

                                     Calculate the cumulative probability of each residual using the formula:

                                               P(i-th residual) = i/(N+1)

                                     with P denoting the cumulative probability of a point, i is the order of the
                                     value in the list and N is the number of entries in the list.

                                     Plot the calculated p-values versus the residual value on normal probability
                                     paper.

                             The normal probability plot should produce an approximately straight line if the
                             points come from a normal distribution.

       Planning            The objectives for an experiment are best determined by a

       experiment          even the "unspoken" ones.

                                  important
                                       when you have 2 - 4 factors and can perform a

                                       when you have more than 3 factors and want to
                                       begin with as small a design as possible (Section
                                       5.3.3.4 and 5.3.3.5)
                                       when you have some qualitative factors, or you
                                       have some quantitative factors that are known to
                                       have a non-monotonic effect (Section 3.3.3.10)

                                  Note that some authors prefer to restrict the term
                                  screening design to the case where you are trying to

                                  design). We include the case with a smaller number of
                                  factors, usually a full factorial design, since the basic
                                  purpose and analysis is similar.

                           Orthogonal Property of Scaling in a 2-Factor Experiment

       Coding              Coding is sometime called "orthogonal coding" since all the columns
       produces            of a coded 2-factor design matrix (except the "I" column) are typically
       orthogonal          orthogonal. That is, the dot product for any pair of columns is zero. For
       columns             example, for X1 and X2: (-1)(-1) + (+1)(-1) + (-1)(+1) + (+1)(+1) = 0.

              design?

      A design is          The choice of an experimental design depends on the
      selected             objectives of the experiment and the number of factors to be
      based on the         investigated.
      experimental
      objective
      and the
      number of

                           Experimental Design Objectives

      Types of             Types of designs are listed here according to the
      designs are          experimental objective they meet.
      listed here
      according to                 Comparative objective: If you have one or several
      the                          factors under investigation, but the primary goal of
      experimental                 your experiment is to make a conclusion about one a-
      objective                    priori important factor, (in the presence of, and/or in
      they meet                    spite of the existence of the other factors), and the
                                   question of interest is whether or not that factor is
                                   "significant", (i.e., whether or not there is a significant
                                   change in the response for different levels of that
                                   factor), then you have a comparative problem and you
                                   need a comparative design solution.

                                   Screening objective: The primary purpose of the
                                   experiment is to select or screen out the few important
                                   main effects from the many less important ones. These
                                   screening designs are also termed main effects
                                   designs.

                                   Response Surface (method) objective: The
                                   experiment is designed to allow us to estimate
                                   interaction and even quadratic effects, and therefore
                                   give us an idea of the (local) shape of the response
                                   surface we are investigating. For this reason, they are
                                   termed response surface method (RSM) designs. RSM
                                   designs are used to:
                                          Find improved or optimal process settings
                                          Troubleshoot process problems and weak points
                                          Make a product or process more robust against

                                            external and non-controllable influences.
                                            "Robust" means relatively insensitive to these
                                            influences.

                                      Optimizing responses when factors are proportions
                                      of a mixture objective: If you have factors that are
                                      proportions of a mixture and you want to know what
                                      the "best" proportions of the factors are so as to
                                      maximize (or minimize) a response, then you need a
                                      mixture design.

                                      Optimal fitting of a regression model objective: If
                                      you want to model a response as a mathematical
                                      function (either known or empirical) of a few
                                      continuous factors and you desire "good" model
                                      parameter estimates (i.e., unbiased and minimum
                                      variance), then you need a regression design.

       5.3.3.1. Completely randomized designs

      These designs           Here we consider completely randomized designs that
      are for                 have one primary factor. The experiment compares the
      studying the            values of a response variable based on the different levels
      effects of one          of that primary factor.
      primary factor
      without the             For completely randomized designs, the levels of the
      need to take            primary factor are randomly assigned to the experimental
      other nuisance          units. By randomization, we mean that the run sequence of
      factors into            the experimental units is determined randomly. For
      account                 example, if there are 3 levels of the primary factor with
                              each level to be run 2 times, then there are 6 factorial
                              possible run sequences (or 6! ways to order the
                              experimental trials). Because of the replication, the
                              number of unique orderings is 90 (since 90 =
                              6!/(2!*2!*2!)). An example of an unrandomized design
                              would be to always run 2 replications for the first level,
                              then 2 for the second level, and finally 2 for the third
                              level. To randomize the runs, one way would be to put 6
                              slips of paper in a box with 2 having level 1, 2 having
                              level 2, and 2 having level 3. Before each run, one of the
                              slips would be drawn blindly from the box and the level
                              selected would be used for the next run of the experiment.

      Randomization           In practice, the randomization is typically performed by a
      typically               computer program. However, the randomization can also
      performed by            be generated from random number tables or by some
      computer                physical mechanism (e.g., drawing the slips of paper).
      software

      Three key               All completely randomized designs with one primary
      numbers                 factor are defined by 3 numbers:

                                     k = number of factors (= 1 for these designs)
                                     L = number of levels
                                     n = number of replications

                              and the total sample size (number of runs) is N = k x L x
                              n.

      Balance                 Balance dictates that the number of replications be the
                              same at each level of the factor (this will maximize the
                              sensitivity of subsequent statistical t (or F) tests).

       5.3.3.2. Randomized block designs

      Blocking to            For randomized block designs, there is one factor or
      "remove" the           variable that is of primary interest. However, there are also
      effect of              several other nuisance factors.
      nuisance
      factors                Nuisance factors are those that may affect the measured
                             result, but are not of primary interest. For example, in
                             applying a treatment, nuisance factors might be the specific
                             operator who prepared the treatment, the time of day the
                             experiment was run, and the room temperature. All
                             experiments have nuisance factors. The experimenter will
                             typically need to spend some time deciding which nuisance
                             factors are important enough to keep track of or control, if
                             possible, during the experiment.

      Blocking used          When we can control nuisance factors, an important
      for nuisance           technique known as blocking can be used to reduce or
      factors that           eliminate the contribution to experimental error contributed
      can be                 by nuisance factors. The basic concept is to create
      controlled             homogeneous blocks in which the nuisance factors are held
                             constant and the factor of interest is allowed to vary.
                             Within blocks, it is possible to assess the effect of different
                             levels of the factor of interest without having to worry
                             about variations due to changes of the block factors, which
                             are accounted for in the analysis.

      Definition of          A nuisance factor is used as a blocking factor if every level
      blocking               of the primary factor occurs the same number of times with
      factors                each level of the nuisance factor. The analysis of the
                             experiment will focus on the effect of varying levels of the
                             primary factor within each block of the experiment.

      Block for a            The general rule is:
      few of the
      most                           "Block what you can, randomize what you cannot."
      important
      nuisance               Blocking is used to remove the effects of a few of the most
      factors                important nuisance variables. Randomization is then used
                             to reduce the contaminating effects of the remaining
                             nuisance variables.

      Table of               One useful way to look at a randomized block experiment
      randomized             is to consider it as a collection of completely randomized

                             Example of a Randomized Block Design

      Example of a           Suppose engineers at a semiconductor manufacturing
      randomized             facility want to test whether different wafer implant
      block design           material dosages have a significant effect on resistivity
                             measurements after a diffusion process taking place in a
                             furnace. They have four different dosages they want to try
                             and enough experimental wafers from the same lot to run
                             three wafers at each of the dosages.

      Furnace run            The nuisance factor they are concerned with is "furnace
      is a nuisance          run" since it is known that each furnace run differs from
      factor                 the last and impacts many process parameters.

      Ideal would            An ideal way to run this experiment would be to run all the
      be to                  4x3=12 wafers in the same furnace run. That would
      eliminate              eliminate the nuisance furnace factor completely. However,
      nuisance               regular production wafers have furnace priority, and only a
      furnace factor         few experimental wafers are allowed into any furnace run
                             at the same time.

      Non-Blocked            A non-blocked way to run this experiment would be to run
      method                 each of the twelve experimental wafers, in random order,


http://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/pri/section3/pri332.htm[6/27/2012 2:23:41 PM]
5.3.3.2. Randomized block designs

                             one per furnace run. That would increase the experimental
                             error of each resistivity measurement by the run-to-run
                             furnace variability and make it more difficult to study the
                             effects of the different dosages. The blocked way to run
                             this experiment, assuming you can convince manufacturing
                             to let you put four experimental wafers in a furnace run,
                             would be to put four wafers with different dosages in each
                             of three furnace runs. The only randomization would be
                             choosing which of the three wafers with dosage 1 would go
                             into furnace run 1, and similarly for the wafers with
                             dosages 2, 3 and 4.

      Description of         Let X1 be dosage "level" and X2 be the blocking factor
      the                    furnace run. Then the experiment can be described as
      experiment             follows:

                                     k = 2 factors (1 primary factor X1 and 1 blocking
                                     factor X2)
                                     L1 = 4 levels of factor X1
                                     L2 = 3 levels of factor X2
                                     n = 1 replication per cell
                                     N =L1 * L2 = 4 * 3 = 12 runs

       5.3.3.2.1. Latin square and related designs

       Latin square            Latin square designs, and the related Graeco-Latin square
       (and related)           and Hyper-Graeco-Latin square designs, are a special type of
       designs are             comparative design.
       efficient
       designs to              There is a single factor of primary interest, typically called
       block from 2            the treatment factor, and several nuisance factors. For Latin
       to 4 nuisance           square designs there are 2 nuisance factors, for Graeco-Latin
       factors                 square designs there are 3 nuisance factors, and for Hyper-
                               Graeco-Latin square designs there are 4 nuisance factors.

       Nuisance                The nuisance factors are used as blocking variables.
       factors used
       as blocking                 1. For Latin square designs, the 2 nuisance factors are
       variables                      divided into a tabular grid with the property that each
                                      row and each column receive each treatment exactly
                                      once.

                                   2. As with the Latin square design, a Graeco-Latin square
                                      design is a kxk tabular grid in which k is the number of
                                      levels of the treatment factor. However, it uses 3
                                      blocking variables instead of the 2 used by the standard
                                      Latin square design.

                                   3. A Hyper-Graeco-Latin square design is also a kxk
                                      tabular grid with k denoting the number of levels of the
                                      treatment factor. However, it uses 4 blocking variables
                                      instead of the 2 used by the standard Latin square
                                      design.


       Advantages              The advantages of Latin square designs are:
       and
       disadvantages               1. They handle the case when we have several nuisance
       of Latin                       factors and we either cannot combine them into a
       square                         single factor or we wish to keep them separate.
       designs
                                   2. They allow experiments with a relatively small number
                                      of runs.

                               The disadvantages are:

                                   1. The number of levels of each blocking variable must

5.3.3.2.1. Latin square and related designs

                                       equal the number of levels of the treatment factor.

                                   2. The Latin square model assumes that there are no
                                      interactions between the blocking variables or between
                                      the treatment variable and the blocking variable.

                               Note that Latin square designs are equivalent to specific
                               fractional factorial designs (e.g., the 4x4 Latin square design
                               is equivalent to a 43-1 fractional factorial design).

       setting of                 `low' or `+1' and `-1', respectively. A design with all
       every factor               possible high/low combinations of all the input factors is
       appears with               called a full factorial design in two levels.
       every setting
       of every other             If there are k factors, each at 2 levels, a full factorial
       factor is a                design has 2k runs.

                                Standard Order for a 2k Level Factorial Design

       Rule for                 We can readily generalize the 23 standard order matrix to a
       writing a 2k             2-level full factorial with k factors. The first (X1) column
       full factorial           starts with -1 and alternates in sign for all 2k runs. The
       in "standard             second (X2) column starts with -1 repeated twice, then
       order"                   alternates with 2 in a row of the opposite sign until all 2k
                                places are filled. The third (X3) column starts with -1
                                repeated 4 times, then 4 repeats of +1's and so on. In general,
                                the i-th column (Xi) starts with 2i-1 repeats of -1 folowed by
                                2i-1 repeats of +1.

       factorial                on product uniformity. Two replications were run at each

       between                  (or suitably chosen fractional) factorial experiment has

       main effects             (except the "I" column) sum to 0.
       and
       interactions             The orthogonality property is important because it eliminates
                                correlation between the estimates of the main effects and
                                interactions.

       An example of            The following is an example of a full factorial design with

       design with 3            added center points.
       factors
                                Suppose that we wish to improve the yield of a polishing
                                operation. The three inputs (factors) that are considered
                                important to the operation are Speed (X1), Feed (X2), and
                                Depth (X3). We want to ascertain the relative importance of
                                each of these factors on Yield (Y).

                                Speed, Feed and Depth can all be varied continuously along
                                their respective scales, from a low to a high setting. Yield is
                                observed to vary smoothly when progressive changes are
                                made to the inputs. This leads us to believe that the ultimate
                                response surface for Y will be smooth.

                                Replication

       Replication              Running the entire design more than once makes for easier
       provides                 data analysis because, for each run (i.e., `corner of the
       information on           design box') we obtain an average value of the response as
       variability              well as some idea about the dispersion (variability,
                                consistency) of the response at that setting.

       Homogeneity              One of the usual analysis assumptions is that the response
       of variance              dispersion is uniform across the experimental space. The
                                technical term is `homogeneity of variance'. Replication
                                allows us to check this assumption and possibly find the
                                setting combinations that give inconsistent yields, allowing
                                us to avoid that area of the factor space.

       Randomization            The more freely one can randomize experimental runs, the
       provides                 more insurance one has against extraneous factors possibly
       protection               affecting the results, and hence perhaps wasting our
       against                  experimental time and effort. For example, consider the
       extraneous               `Depth' column: the settings of Depth, in standard order,
       factors                  follow a `four low, four high, four low, four high' pattern.
       affecting the
       results                  Suppose now that four settings are run in the day and four

                                temperature in the polishing shop affects Yield. We would
                                run the experiment over two days and two nights and
                                conclude that Depth influenced Yield, when in fact ambient
                                temperature was the significant influence. So the moral is:
                                Randomize experimental runs as much as possible.

        5.3.3.3.3. Blocking of full factorial designs

       Eliminate the            We often need to eliminate the influence of extraneous
       influence of             factors when running an experiment. We do this by
       extraneous               "blocking".
       factors by
       "blocking"               Previously, blocking was introduced when randomized
                                block designs were discussed. There we were concerned
                                with one factor in the presence of one of more nuisance
                                factors. In this section we look at a general approach that
                                enables us to divide 2-level factorial experiments into
                                blocks.

                                For example, assume we anticipate predictable shifts will
                                occur while an experiment is being run. This might happen
                                when one has to change to a new batch of raw materials
                                halfway through the experiment. The effect of the change in
                                raw materials is well known, and we want to eliminate its
                                influence on the subsequent data analysis.

       Blocking in a            In this case, we need to divide our experiment into two
       23 factorial             halves (2 blocks), one with the first raw material batch and
       design                   the other with the new batch. The division has to balance
                                out the effect of the materials change in such a way as to
                                eliminate its influence on the analysis, and we do this by
                                blocking.

       Example                  Example: An eight-run 23 full factorial has to be blocked
                                into two groups of four runs each. Consider the design `box'
                                for the 23 full factorial. Blocking can be achieved by
                                assigning the first block to the dark-shaded corners and the
                                second block to the open circle corners.

       interaction              of the (unwanted) blocking effect to the three-factor
       confounded               interaction, and because of the special property of two-level
       with the block           designs called orthogonality. That is, the three-factor
       effect                   interaction is "confounded" with the block effect as will be

       Orthogonality            Orthogonality guarantees that we can always estimate the
                                effect of one factor or interaction clear of any influence due
                                to any other factor or interaction. Orthogonality is a very
                                desirable property in DOE and this is a major reason why
                                two-level factorials are so popular and successful.

       Most DOE                 The general rule for blocking is: use one or a combination
       software will            of high-order interaction columns to construct blocks. This
       do blocking              gives us a formal way of blocking complex designs. Apart
       for you                  from simple cases in which you can design your own

                                asked, but you do need to understand the principle behind

       Block effects            The price you pay for blocking by using high-order
       are                      interaction columns is that you can no longer distinguish the
       confounded               high-order interaction(s) from the blocking effect - they
       with higher-             have been `confounded,' or `aliased.' In fact, the blocking
       order                    effect is now the sum of the blocking effect and the high-
       interactions             order interaction effect. This is fine as long as our
                                assumption about negligible high-order interactions holds
                                true, which it usually does.

       Center points            Within a block, center point runs are assigned as if the
       within a block           block were a separate experiment - which in a sense it is.
                                Randomization takes place within a block as it would for
                                any non-blocked DOE.

      Responses in           The right-most column of the table lists `y 1 ' through `y 8 ' to
      standard               indicate the responses measured for the experimental runs
      order                  when listed in standard order. For example, `y 1 ' is the
                             response (i.e., output) observed when the three factors were
                             all run at their `low' setting. The numbers entered in the "y"
                             column will be used to illustrate calculations of effects.

      Computing X1           From the entries in the table we are able to compute all
      main effect            `effects' such as main effects, first-order `interaction'
                             effects, etc. For example, to compute the main effect
                             estimate `c 1 ' of factor X1 , we compute the average response
                             at all runs with X1 at the `high' setting, namely (1/4)(y 2 +
                             y 4 + y 6 + y 8 ), minus the average response of all runs with
                             X1 set at `low,' namely (1/4)(y 1 + y 3 + y 5 + y 7 ). That is,

                                     c 1 = (1/4) (y 2 + y 4 + y 6 + y 8 ) - (1/4)(y 1 + y 3 + y 5 +
                                     y 7 ) or
                                     c 1 = (1/4)(63+57+51+53 ) - (1/4)(33+41+57+59) =
                                     8.5


      Can we                 Suppose, however, that we only have enough resources to
      estimate X1            do four runs. Is it still possible to estimate the main effect
      main effect            for X1 ? Or any other main effect? The answer is yes, and
      with four              there are even different choices of the four runs that will
      runs?                  accomplish this.

      Example of             For example, suppose we select only the four light
      computing the          (unshaded) corners of the design cube. Using these four
      main effects           runs (1, 4, 6 and 7), we can still compute c 1 as follows:
      using only
      four runs                      c 1 = (1/2) (y 4 + y 6 ) - (1/2) (y 1 + y 7 ) or
                                     c 1 = (1/2) (57+51) - (1/2) (33+59) = 8.

                             Simarly, we would compute c 2 , the effect due to X2 , as

                                     c 2 = (1/2) (y 4 + y 7 ) - (1/2) (y 1 + y 6 ) or
                                     c 2 = (1/2) (57+59) - (1/2) (33+51) = 16.

                                     c 3 = (1/2) (y 6 + y 7 ) - (1/2) (y 1 + y 4 ) or

      Alternative            We could also have used the four dark (shaded) corners of
      runs for               the design cube for our runs and obtained similiar, but
      computing              slightly different, estimates for the main effects. In either
      main effects           case, we would have used half the number of runs that the
                             full factorial requires. The half fraction we used is a new
                             design written as 23-1 . Note that 23-1 = 23 /2 = 22 = 4,
                             which is the number of runs in this half-fraction design. In
                             the next section, a general method for choosing fractions
                             that "work" will be discussed.

      Example of              Example: An engineering experiment calls for running
      how                    three factors, namely Pressure, Table speed, and Down
      fractional             force, each at a `high' and a `low' setting, on a production
      factorial              tool to determine which has the greatest effect on product
      experiments            uniformity. Interaction effects are considered negligible, but
      often arise in         uniformity measurement error requires that at least two
      industry               separate runs (replications) be made at each process setting.
                             In addition, several `standard setting' runs (centerpoint runs)
                             need to be made at regular intervals during the experiment
                             to monitor for process drift. As experimental time and
                             material are limited, no more than 15 runs can be planned.

                             A full factorial 23 design, replicated twice, calls for 8x2 =
                             16 runs, even without centerpoint runs, so this is not an
                             option. However a 23-1 design replicated twice requires
                             only 4x2 = 8 runs, and then we would have 15-8 = 7 spare
                             runs: 3 to 5 of these spare runs can be used for centerpoint
                             runs and the rest saved for backup in case something goes
                             wrong with any run. As long as we are confident that the
                             interactions are negligbly small (compared to the main
                             effects), and as long as complete replication is required,
                             then the above replicated 23-1 fractional factorial design
                             (with center points) is a very reasonable choice.

                             On the other hand, if interactions are potentially large (and
                             if the replication required could be set aside), then the usual
                             23 full factorial design (with center points) would serve as a
                             good design.

       5.3.3.4.3. Confounding (also called aliasing)

       Confounding            One price we pay for using the design table column X1*X2 to
       means we               obtain column X3 in Table 3.14 is, clearly, our inability to obtain
       have lost the          an estimate of the interaction effect for X1*X2 (i.e., c 12) that is
       ability to             separate from an estimate of the main effect for X3. In other
       estimate               words, we have confounded the main effect estimate for factor
       some effects           X3 (i.e., c 3 ) with the estimate of the interaction effect for X1 and
       and/or                 X2 (i.e., with c 12). The whole issue of confounding is
       interactions
                              fundamental to the construction of fractional factorial designs,
                              and we will spend time discussing it below.

       Sparsity of            In using the 23-1 design, we also assume that c 12 is small
       effects                compared to c 3 ; this is called a `sparsity of effects' assumption.
       assumption
                              Our computation of c 3 is in fact a computation of c 3 + c 12. If the
                              desired effects are only confounded with non-significant
                              interactions, then we are OK.

                              A Notation and Method for Generating Confounding or
                              Aliasing

       A short way            A short way of writing `X3 = X1*X2' (understanding that we are
       of writing             talking about multiplying columns of the design table together)
       factor                 is: `3 = 12' (similarly 3 = -12 refers to X3 = -X1*X2). Note that
       column                 `12' refers to column multiplication of the kind we are using to
       multiplication         construct the fractional design and any column multiplied by
                              itself gives the identity column of all 1's.

                              Next we multiply both sides of 3=12 by 3 and obtain 33=123, or
                              I=123 since 33=I (or a column of all 1's). Playing around with
                              this "algebra", we see that 2I=2123, or 2=2123, or 2=1223, or
                              2=13 (since 2I=2, 22=I, and 1I3=13). Similarly, 1=23.

       Definition of          I=123 is called a design generator or a generating relation for
       "design                this 23-1 design (the dark-shaded corners of Figure 3.4). Since
       generator" or          there is only one design generator for this design, it is also the
       "generating            defining relation for the design. Equally, I=-123 is the design
       relation" and          generator (and defining relation) for the light-shaded corners of
       "defining              Figure 3.4. We call I=123 the defining relation for the 23-1
       relation"              design because with it we can generate (by "multiplication") the


http://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/pri/section3/pri3343.htm[6/27/2012 2:23:56 PM]
5.3.3.4.3. Confounding (also called aliasing)

                              complete confounding pattern for the design. That is, given
                              I=123, we can generate the set of {1=23, 2=13, 3=12, I=123},
                              which is the complete set of aliases, as they are called, for this
                              23-1 fractional factorial design. With I=123, we can easily
                              generate all the columns of the half-fraction design 23-1 .

       Principal              Note: We can replace any design generator by its negative
       fraction               counterpart and have an equivalent, but different fractional
                              design. The fraction generated by positive design generators is
                              sometimes called the principal fraction.

       All main               The confounding pattern described by 1=23, 2=13, and 3=12
       effects of 23-1        tells us that all the main effects of the 23-1 design are confounded
       design                 with two-factor interactions. That is the price we pay for using
       confounded             this fractional design. Other fractional designs have different
       with two-              confounding patterns; for example, in the typical quarter-fraction
       factor                 of a 26 design, i.e., in a 26-2 design, main effects are confounded
       interactions           with three-factor interactions (e.g., 5=123) and so on. In the case
                              of 5=123, we can also readily see that 15=23 (etc.), which alerts
                              us to the fact that certain two-factor interactions of a 26-2 are
                              confounded with other two-factor interactions.

                             these original three words. These seven turn out to be I =
                             3456 = 12457 = 12358 = 12367 = 12468 = 3478 = 5678. In
                             general, there will be (2 p -1) words in the defining relation
                             for a 2k-p fractional factorial.

       Definition of         The length of the shortest word in the defining relation is
       "Resolution"          called the resolution of the design. Resolution describes the
                             degree to which estimated main effects are aliased (or
                             confounded) with estimated 2-level interactions, 3-level
                             interactions, etc.

       and                   confounded. Previously, in the 23-1 design, we saw that the
       confounding           main effects were confounded with two-factor interactions.
                             However, main effects were not confounded with other main

                             Design Resolution Summary

       Commonly              The meaning of the most prevalent resolution levels is as
       used design           follows:
       Resolutions
                                                       Resolution III Designs

                             Main effects are confounded (aliased) with two-factor
                             interactions.

                                                        Resolution IV Designs

                             No main effects are aliased with two-factor interactions, but
                             two-factor interactions are aliased with each other.

                                                        Resolution V Designs

                             No main effect or two-factor interaction is aliased with any
                             other main effect or two-factor interaction, but two-factor
                             interactions are aliased with three-factor interactions.

        5.3.3.4.5. Use of fractional factorial designs

       Use low-                  The basic purpose of a fractional factorial design is to
       resolution                economically investigate cause-and-effect relationships of
       designs for               significance in a given experimental setting. This does not
       screening                 differ in essence from the purpose of any experimental
       among main                design. However, because we are able to choose fractions
       effects and use           of a full design, and hence be more economical, we also
       higher-                   have to be aware that different factorial designs serve
       resolution                different purposes.
       designs when
       interaction               Broadly speaking, with designs of resolution three, and
       effects and               sometimes four, we seek to screen out the few important
       response                  main effects from the many less important others. For this
       surfaces need             reason, these designs are often termed main effects
       to be                     designs, or screening designs.
       investigated
                                 On the other hand, designs of resolution five, and higher,
                                 are used for focusing on more than just main effects in an
                                 experimental situation. These designs allow us to estimate
                                 interaction effects and such designs are easily augmented
                                 to complete a second-order design - a design that permits
                                 estimation of a full second-order (quadratic) model.

       Different                 Within the screening/RSM strategy of design, there are a
       purposes for              number of functional purposes for which designs are used.
       screening/RSM             For example, an experiment might be designed to
       designs                   determine how to make a product better or a process more
                                 robust against the influence of external and non-
                                 controllable influences such as the weather. Experiments
                                 might be designed to troubleshoot a process, to determine
                                 bottlenecks, or to specify which component(s) of a product
                                 are most in need of improvement. Experiments might also
                                 be designed to optimize yield, or to minimize defect
                                 levels, or to move a process away from an unstable
                                 operating zone. All these aims and purposes can be
                                 achieved using fractional factorial designs and their
                                 appropriate design enhancements.

       Screening           The term `Screening Design' refers to an experimental plan
       designs are         that is intended to find the few significant factors from a list
       an efficient        of many potential ones. Alternatively, we refer to a design as
       way to              a screening design if its primary purpose is to identify
       identify            significant main effects, rather than interaction effects, the
       significant         latter being assumed an order of magnitude less important.
       main effects

       screening           response surface model (an RSM analysis), the first
       designs             experiment should be a screening design when there are
       when you            many factors to consider.
       have many
       factors to
       consider

       Screening           Screening designs are typically of resolution III. The reason is
       designs are         that resolution III designs permit one to explore the effects of
       usually             many factors with an efficient number of runs.
       resolution
       III or IV           Sometimes designs of resolution IV are also used for
                           screening designs. In these designs, main effects are
                           confounded with, at worst, three-factor interactions. This is
                           better from the confounding viewpoint, but the designs
                           require more runs than a resolution III design.

       Plackett-           Another common family of screening designs is the Plackett-
       Burman              Burman set of designs, so named after its inventors. These
       designs             designs are of resolution III and will be described later.

       Economical          In short, screening designs are economical experimental plans
       plans for           that focus on determining the relative significance of many
       determing           main effects.

      Plackett-           In 1946, R.L. Plackett and J.P. Burman published their now famous paper "The Design
      Burman              of Optimal Multifactorial Experiments" in Biometrika (vol. 33). This paper described the
      designs             construction of very economical designs with the run number a multiple of four (rather
                          than a power of 2). Plackett-Burman designs are very efficient screening designs when
                          only main effects are of interest.

       5.3.3.6.4. Blocking a response surface design

                            How can we block a response surface design?

       When                 If an investigator has run either a 2k full factorial or a 2k-p fractional
       augmenting           factorial design of at least resolution V, augmentation of that design
       a resolution         to a central composite design (either CCC of CCF) is easily
       V design to          accomplished by adding an additional set (block) of star and
       a CCC                centerpoint runs. If the factorial experiment indicated (via the t test)
       design by            curvature, this composite augmentation is the best follow-up option
       adding star          (follow-up options for other situations will be discussed later).
       points, it
       may be
       desirable to
       block the
       design

       An                   An important point to take into account when choosing a response
       orthogonal           surface design is the possibility of running the design in blocks.
       blocked              Blocked designs are better designs if the design allows the estimation
       response             of individual and interaction factor effects independently of the block
       surface              effects. This condition is called orthogonal blocking. Blocks are
       design has           assumed to have no impact on the nature and shape of the response
       advantages           surface.

       CCF                  The CCF design does not allow orthogonal blocking and the Box-
       designs              Behnken designs offer blocking only in limited circumstances,
       cannot be            whereas the CCC does permit orthogonal blocking.
       orthogonally
       blocked

       Axial and            In general, when two blocks are required there should be an axial
       factorial            block and a factorial block. For three blocks, the factorial block is
       blocks               divided into two blocks and the axial block is not split. The blocking
                            of the factorial design points should result in orthogonality between
                            blocks and individual factors and between blocks and the two factor
                            interactions.

       5.3.3.7. Adding centerpoints

                           Center point, or `Control' Runs

       Centerpoint         As mentioned earlier in this section, we add centerpoint runs
       runs                interspersed among the experimental setting runs for two
       provide a           purposes:
       check for
       both                           1. To provide a measure of process stability
       process                           and inherent variability
       stability and                  2. To check for curvature.
       possible
       curvature

       Centerpoint         Centerpoint runs should begin and end the experiment, and
       runs are not        should be dispersed as evenly as possible throughout the
       randomized          design matrix. The centerpoint runs are not randomized!
                           There would be no reason to randomize them as they are
                           there as guardians against process instability and the best way
                           to find instability is to sample the process on a regular basis.

       Rough rule          With this in mind, we have to decide on how many
       of thumb is         centerpoint runs to do. This is a tradeoff between the
       to add 3 to         resources we have, the need for enough runs to see if there is
       5 center            process instability, and the desire to get the experiment over
       point runs          with as quickly as possible. As a rough guide, you should
       to your             generally add approximately 3 to 5 centerpoint runs to a full
       design              or fractional factorial design.

                           Pseudo Center points

       Center              One often runs experiments in which some factors are
       points for          nominal. For example, Catalyst "A" might be the (-1) setting,
       discrete            catalyst "B" might be coded (+1). The choice of which is
       factors             "high" and which is "low" is arbitrary, but one must have
                           some way of deciding which catalyst setting is the "standard"
                           one.

                           These standard settings for the discrete input factors together
                           with center points for the continuous input factors, will be
                           regarded as the "center points" for purposes of design.

                               Center Points in Response Surface Designs

       Uniform             In an unblocked response surface design, the number of
       precision           center points controls other properties of the design matrix.
                           The number of center points can make the design orthogonal
                           or have "uniform precision." We will only focus on uniform
                           precision here as classical quadratic designs were set up to
                           have this property.

       Variance of         Uniform precision ensures that the variance of prediction is
       prediction          the same at the center of the experimental space as it is at a
                           unit distance away from the center.

       Protection          In a response surface context, to contrast the virtue of
       against bias        uniform precision designs over replicated center-point
                           orthogonal designs one should also consider the following
                           guidance from Montgomery ("Design and Analysis of
                           Experiments," Wiley, 1991, page 547), "A uniform precision
                           design offers more protection against bias in the regression
                           coefficients than does an orthogonal design because of the
                           presence of third-order and higher terms in the true surface.

       Controlling         Myers, Vining, et al, ["Variance Dispersion of Response
         and the           Surface Designs," Journal of Quality Technology, 24, pp. 1-
       number of           11 (1992)] have explored the options regarding the number of
       center              center points and the value of somewhat further: An
       points              investigator may control two parameters, and the number
                           of center points (nc), given k factors. Either set = 2(k/4)

        5.3.3.9. Three-level full factorial designs

       Three-level              The three-level design is written as a 3k factorial design. It means
       designs are              that k factors are considered, each at 3 levels. These are (usually)
       useful for               referred to as low, intermediate and high levels. These levels are
       investigating            numerically expressed as 0, 1, and 2. One could have considered the
       quadratic                digits -1, 0, and +1, but this may be confusing with respect to the 2-
       effects                  level designs since 0 is reserved for center points. Therefore, we will
                                use the 0, 1, 2 scheme. The reason that the three-level designs were
                                proposed is to model possible curvature in the response function and
                                to handle the case of nominal factors at 3 levels. A third level for a
                                continuous factor facilitates investigation of a quadratic relationship
                                between the response and each of the factors.

       Three-level              Unfortunately, the three-level design is prohibitive in terms of the
       design may               number of runs, and thus in terms of cost and effort. For example a
       require                  two-level design with center points is much less expensive while it
       prohibitive              still is a very good (and simple) way to establish the presence or
       number of                absence of curvature.
       runs

                                The 32 design

       The simplest             This is the simplest three-level design. It has two factors, each at
       3-level design           three levels. The 9 treatment combinations for this type of design can
       - with only 2            be shown pictorially as follows:
       factors

5.3.3.9. Three-level full factorial designs




                                A notation such as "20" means that factor A is at its high level (2)
                                and factor B is at its low level (0).

                                The 33 design

       The model                This is a design that consists of three factors, each at three levels. It
       and treatment            can be expressed as a 3 x 3 x 3 = 33 design. The model for such an
       runs for a 3             experiment is
       factor, 3-level
       design



                                where each factor is included as a nominal factor rather than as a
                                continuous variable. In such cases, main effects have 2 degrees of
                                freedom, two-factor interactions have 22 = 4 degrees of freedom and
                                k-factor interactions have 2k degrees of freedom. The model contains
                                2 + 2 + 2 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 8 = 26 degrees of freedom. Note that if there
                                is no replication, the fit is exact and there is no error term (the
                                epsilon term) in the model. In this no replication case, if one assumes
                                that there are no three-factor interactions, then one can use these 8
                                degrees of freedom for error estimation.

                                In this model we see that i = 1, 2, 3, and similarly for j and k, making
                                27 treatments.
